Reclaiming our rivers. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The identification of 224 pollution outlets discharging waste into the Buriganga and Turag rivers should alarm and anger us, yet it is an important and overdue step that also deserves credit.
That the authorities concerned can finally see a clear map of where the damage is happening to two of our most important rivers is a step in the right direction. Acknowledging the problem with precision was needed long ago.
However, this identification also underscores a hard truth: Bangladesh’s rivers will not recover through surveys alone and cleaning them up is not a short‑term fix but a long, disciplined effort that must begin now.
On this note, we admire the realism displayed by Environment Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo who acknowledged that restoring the rivers would take time. We also agree that even a 10% improvement by the end of the year would be considered a success.
The path forward, therefore, requires commitments that must begin with uncompromising enforcement of existing laws. Now that the outlets have been identified, shutting them down cannot be symbolic, and factories dumping waste must face real penalties.
Pollution‑control infrastructure must also actually work. Effluent treatment plants cannot remain idle installations, and there must be a concerted effort to ensure their functionality, in addition to having sewer systems that are redesigned to make sure that waste does not flow directly into rivers.
Identifying these outlets is a positive step, but is only the first step. We must now commit to the long, difficult work of restoring our rivers. It is time for immediate and consistent action to ensure that we are truly serious about reclaiming our rivers.

item.title: Preserving access to justice. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The decision to restrict journalists from entering Supreme Court courtrooms is deeply concerning and warrants immediate reconsideration.
Since January 7, journalists have reportedly been denied access to various courtrooms, including the Appellate Division, preventing them from directly observing proceedings and reporting on cases of immense public importance.
The judiciary is one of the most important pillars of a democratic state, and its legitimacy depends not only on the fairness of its decisions but also on public confidence in the process through which those decisions are reached.
Open court proceedings are therefore an essential mechanism of transparency and accountability.
The media serves as the bridge between institutions and citizens. Most people cannot attend court proceedings themselves, nor can they scrutinize complex legal arguments and judgments -- they depend on journalists to accurately convey what happens inside courtrooms.
Preventing journalists from witnessing proceedings first-hand inevitably weakens that process, and risks creating unnecessary suspicion about what is taking place behind closed doors.
This is particularly troubling at a time when Bangladesh is attempting to strengthen democratic institutions and restore public faith in the rule of law.
The country has already experienced the damaging consequences of restrictions on press freedom, with journalists facing intimidation, attacks, and other forms of pressure in recent years.
Security and administrative concerns can certainly justify reasonable rules governing courtroom access. However, such measures must be transparent, proportionate, and consistent with constitutional principles.
A blanket or prolonged restriction on journalists cannot become the default solution.
The Supreme Court should, therefore, engage constructively with the protesting journalists and establish clear guidelines that protect both courtroom decorum and media access. Restoring journalists' access would not amount to conceding to pressure; rather, it would demonstrate confidence in the judiciary and its proceedings.
An open justice system should have nothing to fear from scrutiny. If Bangladesh is serious about strengthening democracy, transparency inside its highest court must be treated as a principle.

item.title: Between departure and the hope of homecoming. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Colourful toy boxes peeked out from the shopping bags they clutched. They wore impatient smiles, eager to board the flight.
The heavy backpacks and carefully packed shopping bags caught my attention first. Then there were the vibrant fleece blankets. Somehow, they too had become part of the journey home for Bangladeshi migrant workers. Watching them, I found myself rewinding to where their journeys had begun.
A few days earlier, at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka, I had stood in the immigration queue for my own flight to Malaysia.
"First time?" the immigration officer asked with a smile.
I nodded.
As I moved ahead, my attention drifted to the queue behind me. Timid eyes searched for reassurance. Some looked restless, others uncertain, quietly waiting for instructions that never came.
Many were first-time travellers navigating an unfamiliar process with little guidance. For those who had perhaps never travelled beyond their own districts, an international airport could feel overwhelming.
Yet the warmth and patience extended to many travellers seemed to disappear when it came to those who arguably needed it the most.
This stayed with me.
Safe migration does not begin when a worker lands at their destination; it begins the moment they leave home. A migrant-friendly departure process, clearer guidance at airports, and greater sensitivity from frontline officials are not extraordinary expectations. They are simple yet meaningful ways of recognizing that for many of these workers, this journey is both unfamiliar and life-changing.
These were the very people who had left behind ageing parents, spouses, and children in pursuit of a better future. They were leaving not for adventure, but for responsibility.
Their sacrifices sustain countless families, and their earnings quietly strengthen Bangladesh's economy. We proudly celebrate them as our remittance warriors . But how often do we pause to see the people behind that title?
Bangladeshis constitute nearly 37% of Malaysia's foreign workforce, with more than 800,000 holding valid employment permits as of June 2025. The figures often dominate headlines, reflecting the scale of labour migration between the two countries. Yet behind every number is a life suspended between two homes, two realities, and often, two versions of oneself.
It was only after arriving in Malaysia that those faces began to reappear.
In Johor Bahru, Bangladeshi workers seemed to be everywhere in hotels, Airbnb properties, restaurants, construction sites, and the countless neighbourhood car washes that keep the city moving. Their presence was unmistakable, yet strangely invisible. They worked quietly, efficiently, almost anonymously.
What stayed with me, however, was not where I found them, but their faces.
I searched for signs of ease, of contentment, of belonging. Instead, I saw exhaustion etched into expressions that had grown accustomed to demanding days. Occasionally, a smile surfaced, but it disappeared almost as quickly as it appeared, swallowed by another task waiting to be done.
Those faces followed me long after I left Johor Bahru. They stayed with me in Kuala Lumpur, quietly shaping the way I looked at every Bangladeshi worker I passed.
One afternoon, two men struggled to push a trolley stacked high with heavy cartons up an inclined road. The load was clearly meant for more than two pairs of hands.
" Jaan bair hoya jaitese bhai, ar mone hoy parum na ", one of them gasped as he paused to catch his breath.
For a fleeting moment, they smiled at each other before pushing forward again.
That smile lingered with me. It carried resilience more than relief, a quiet acceptance that there was work to finish, another shift to begin, another day to endure.
The uncertainty I had witnessed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport did not end once the flight landed. It simply changed its form. In Johor Bahru, it appeared in weary faces that had grown accustomed to long days of demanding work. In Kuala Lumpur, it resurfaced in the quiet apprehension that seemed to accompany even their journey home.
Behind these moments lie deeper structural challenges, exploitative recruitment practices, inadequate orientation before departure, poor living conditions, delayed wages, and limited avenues for seeking justice when rights are violated. Migration should never require workers to navigate these vulnerabilities on their own.
Malaysia remains the second-largest destination for Bangladeshi migrant workers. Although labour recruitment has faced repeated disruptions since June 2024, discussions surrounding the reopening of the labour market have largely centred on the number of workers who can leave, when recruitment will resume, and how quickly demand can be met.
Yet reopening a labour market cannot be the destination in itself.
The success of labour migration should not be measured solely by the number of workers who leave or the remittances they send home. It should also be measured by how safely they migrate, how fairly they are treated while abroad, and whether they can return home with the dignity they left with.
This calls for ethical recruitment, transparent recruitment costs, stronger bilateral oversight, accessible grievance mechanisms, and sustained protection of workers' rights throughout the migration cycle. Opportunity should never come at the cost of dignity.
A few days later, as I stood in the departure queue at Kuala Lumpur International Airport, preparing to return home, I found myself surrounded by those familiar faces once again.
Every kilogram of the hand-carry allowance seemed carefully accounted for. Heavy backpacks strained tired shoulders that, I imagined, had carried far heavier burdens over the years than the permitted seven kilograms.
Then came the weighing scale. For many passengers, it was merely another airport procedure. For them, it seemed to carry an entirely different weight.
One man quietly explained to the immigration staff that the metal tin in his luggage contained powdered milk for his son. There was no frustration in his voice, only the hope that he would be allowed to take it home. For that moment, the baggage no longer seemed heavy.
Each suitcase carried months, sometimes years, of sacrifice transformed into gifts that could never fully measure the distance travelled to earn them. Chocolates, toys, blankets, clothes, powdered milk, ordinary objects made extraordinary by the lives behind them.
They were reminders that while migrant workers often return carrying gifts, they also carry stories that remain largely untold.
Some return to joyful reunions.
Some return with little to show after being deceived or exploited.
Some never return at all.
Watching them, I realized I had spent only a few years working in the migration sector, reading reports, analyzing data. Yet it took standing beside them in airport queues, watching them navigate unfamiliar systems, and witnessing the quiet weight they carried to understand that migration is, above all, profoundly human.
Their resilience cannot and should not be measured solely in remittance figures. It lives in every goodbye they endure, every shift they complete, every burden they quietly shoulder, and every journey they make in the hope of building a better future for those waiting at home.
As boarding began, I watched them once more.
Colourful toy boxes peeked out from the shopping bags they clutched. They wore the same impatient smile, eager to board the flight.
After all, they were finally going home to their loved ones.
Efrita Jahan is currently part of the BRAC Migration Program.

item.title: Are India and Bangladesh finally building the right kind of momentum?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There are moments in diplomacy when individual meetings matter less for what is said behind closed doors than for the pattern they collectively create. India and Bangladesh may be entering precisely such a moment.
On Monday, Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi met Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman in Dhaka. Rahman spoke of creating a conducive environment for improving bilateral relations. On the same day, another significant engagement was taking place in the Bangladeshi capital, India’s Research and Analysis Wing chief Parag Jain met the Prime Minister’s Defence Affairs Adviser, Brigadier General (Retd.) Dr AKM Shamsul Islam.
Viewed separately, these could be treated as routine diplomatic and security engagements. Viewed together with developments over the past six months, however, they point towards something more important: New Delhi and Dhaka are rebuilding a relationship through sustained institutional contact rather than waiting for every political disagreement to disappear.
That is exactly the right approach.
India moved quickly after Bangladesh’s February election. Prime Minister Narendra Modi congratulated Tarique Rahman on his electoral victory and spoke to him directly, reaffirming India’s commitment to the peace, progress and prosperity of both countries. More importantly, India signalled that it was prepared to work with Bangladesh’s new political reality rather than remain trapped in the politics of the past.
That message was reinforced when Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla travelled to Dhaka for Rahman’s swearing-in and carried a personal letter from Modi inviting the new Bangladeshi PM to visit India. This demonstrated that New Delhi wanted political engagement with the new government to begin immediately and at a high level.
The traffic has moved in both directions.
In April, Bangladesh Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman travelled to India and met External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar. He also held meetings with National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Petroleum and Natural Gas Minister Hardeep Singh Puri. India reiterated its desire to engage constructively with Bangladesh’s new government, while both sides agreed to explore proposals for deepening the partnership through existing bilateral mechanisms.
This is particularly important because India-Bangladesh relations cannot be managed exclusively through prime ministerial summits. A mature relationship requires multiple channels operating simultaneously: Political, diplomatic, economic, security, border management, and people-to-people.
That institutional architecture is now visibly returning.
In June, senior officers of the Border Security Force and Border Guard Bangladesh met in New Delhi for their director-general-level conference. The border remains one of the most sensitive areas in bilateral relations, with disagreements over killings, illegal crossings, smuggling and movement across the frontier. Yet precisely because disagreements exist, keeping the two forces talking is essential.
An equally important breakthrough came on the people-to-people front. In June, India announced the resumption of tourist visas for Bangladeshi nationals after a suspension lasting nearly two years. High Commissioner Trivedi announced the move during a visit to the Indian Visa Application Centre in Dhaka. Restoring ordinary travel matters enormously in a relationship where families, businesses, students, patients and cultural networks routinely cross the border.
The Jain-Islam meeting adds another layer to this process. Security cooperation between India and Bangladesh has historically been one of the quiet foundations of bilateral stability. The fact that senior security officials are engaging while diplomatic channels are simultaneously active suggests that the relationship is being rebuilt across institutions rather than around personalities alone.
This does not mean the relationship is suddenly free of problems.
The Sheikh Hasina issue remains deeply contentious. Dhaka has sought her extradition, while India has said the matter is being considered through its legal processes. Water sharing, particularly the future of the Ganges Water Sharing Treaty, border management and trade irritants also require careful negotiation.
But successful diplomacy is not the absence of disagreements. It is the ability to prevent disagreements from consuming the entire relationship.
Geography makes estrangement between India and Bangladesh extraordinarily costly. Bangladesh sits at the heart of India’s connectivity with its Northeast. India surrounds Bangladesh on three sides and remains an indispensable economic, energy, and connectivity partner. The two countries share rivers, a vast border, transport networks, electricity links, cultural connections, and intertwined security interests.
There is therefore a simple strategic reality that governments in both capitals eventually must confront: Neither country gains from prolonged hostility.
The challenge now is to convert the current momentum into deliverables.
Visa normalization should continue. Border mechanisms should meet regularly. Trade bottlenecks should be addressed. Energy cooperation should be expanded. Connectivity projects linking Bangladesh with India’s Northeast and the wider Bay of Bengal economy should regain momentum. Water negotiations must be pursued seriously rather than allowed to become instruments of nationalist politics.
Most importantly, Prime Minister Rahman and Prime Minister Modi should meet when circumstances permit. India’s invitation provides an opportunity to move the reset from official-level engagement to political ownership at the highest level.
The emerging sequence is encouraging: Modi reaching out after the election, Birla travelling to Dhaka, Bangladesh’s foreign minister engaging New Delhi, border forces returning to structured dialogue, tourist visas resuming, Trivedi meeting Rahman, and now senior security officials talking directly.
No single meeting can transform India-Bangladesh relations. But diplomacy is built through accumulation.
One conversation creates space for the next; political contact enables bureaucratic engagement; security dialogue builds confidence; easier visas reconnect societies; and economic cooperation creates constituencies that have a stake in stability.
That is why the developments in Dhaka this week matter. India and Bangladesh do not need a dramatic declaration of friendship. They need sustained, pragmatic, and institutional engagement.
For the first time in some time, that machinery appears to be moving again, and in the right direction.
Rishi Suri is the chief editor at The Daily Milap, one of India’s oldest and largest Urdu newspapers.
